newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya prepares budget amid election jitters.
newsitem.headline: Kenya prepares budget amid election jitters.

text.p: Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi will present Kenya's 1997/98 budget on Thursday against a background of election jitters, drought and persistent government failure to meet many of its economic pledges.

Financial experts and diplomats said on Tuesday that presidential and parliamentary elections that must be held in the 1997 calendar year posed the biggest headache for the government of President Daniel arap Moi.
Violence and widespread economic mismanagement dominated the run-up to the last general elections in 1992. Despite government pledges to the contrary, investors see a repeat performance.
Growing indiscipline still meant that government spending was well beyond forecasts and corruption still hindered revenue collection in areas such as customs, they told Reuters.
Moi has vowed to fight corruption in government but high-level prosecutions are still scarce.
Dennis Kabaara of business firm Coopers & Lybrand said Kenya's problem was its habit of not meeting its forecasts.
The government has issued an economic survey that predicts gross domestic product (GDP) growth at 5.2 percent in 1997/98 compared to 4.9 percent in 1996/97 and 4.8 percent in 1995/96.
"This is at once a challenging and depressing statistic. It is a challenge in that we have now got the habit of not meeting our forecasts," Kabaara wrote in the Daily Nation newspaper.
World Bank Vice-President for Africa Callisto Madavo last month told Reuters that Kenya was guilty of consistently under-performing given its potential and political stability.

Kabaara questioned whether that GDP growth statistic took into account drought that hit most of East Africa in the first quarter of the year, population growth of just under 3.0 percent a year and the ever increasing gap between Kenya's wealthy and poor.

Kabaara said inflation was showing growth tendencies and interest rates were still very high. Inflation has jumped above the government's long-cherished single-digit target and lending rates for commercial banks lie in the 25-35 percent range.
But he saw the budget deficit as being under control, at 1.4 percent of GDP and 3.6 percent of total government expenditure.
Ordinary Kenyans complained of government wastage at many levels. Senior public servants and ministers have a large fleet of official limousines and the president has a large entourage.
Flashy first class travel, huge entertainment and other allowances are seen by some as an encouragement for abuse in government.
In neighbouring Uganda for instance, a minister is allowed one official car and may take a loan to purchase another.
Economic analysts called for streamlining of taxes to avoid double taxation and lowering maximum income tax levied on high earners and which currently stands at around 37 percent.
Financial experts said they wanted measures to stabilise economic growth, stem growth in money supply and maintain a stable exchange rate against the dollar in an election year.

They cited economically suicidal policies in the runup to landmark pluralist elections in 1992 which saw inflation soar to 101 percent and interest rates reach 90 percent on the back of money supply growth of around 33 percent.
Failure of seasonal short rains and late arrival of long rains in parts of Kenya has affected production of main commodity export coffee and staple foods such as maize.

Privatisations through the Nairobi Stock Exchange appear slow and there is still no law to allow a launch of a central depository system that will speed up payments on the bourse. The budget may shed some light on these, brokers said.
